title: New York City Lawmakers Push to ‘Ban the Scan’ at MSG
gist: New York City Council member Shahana Hanif's 'Ban the Scan' bill, which would prohibit biometric recognition tech at public venues, has secured 27 co-endorsements — a City Council majority — and is now in advancement talks with Speaker Julie Menin, directly targeting Madison Square Garden's facial-recognition watch-list system. The push follows WIRED reporting that MSG maintains risk-score dossiers on ~400 celebrities and VIPs, after which MSG sued WIRED for defamation.

insights.claim: A New York City Council bill introduced in January by member Shahana Hanif would prohibit public venues from using biometric recognition technology such as facial recognition, and has now collected 27 endorsements — more than half of the City Council.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: A majority co-sponsor count moves a municipal biometrics ban from advocacy to plausible law; venue operators, stadium security vendors and facial-recognition suppliers with NYC exposure should be watched for a compliance shock.
insights.quote: Hanif’s “Ban the Scan” bill now has 27 endorsements, more than half of the City Council.
insights.locator: Hanif's 'Ban the Scan' bill now has 27

insights.claim: Advancement of the New York City biometric-recognition ban now depends on City Council Speaker Julie Menin, with whom members are in talks to move the legislation, per bill sponsor Shahana Hanif.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: The Speaker is the single gating actor — a scheduling decision by Menin, not further co-sponsorship, is the catalyst to watch for timing.
insights.locator: Members are in talks with speaker Julie Menin

insights.claim: The campaign against venue facial recognition is being driven by a coalition of a sitting city legislator, working musicians and digital-rights groups including Fight for the Future and NYC DSA Tech Action, rallying physically outside Madison Square Garden.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Artist participation raises the reputational cost of biometric screening for venue owners, since talent boycotts are a faster-acting lever than legislation.
insights.locator: At the rally on Friday, Hanif was joined

insights.claim: Madison Square Garden operates an extensive facial-recognition database that has been used to place fans critical of owner James Dolan or of the New York Knicks onto watch lists, according to prior WIRED reporting.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Using biometrics for viewpoint-based exclusion rather than security is the fact pattern most likely to trigger legislative and litigation risk for venue operators.
insights.locator: Madison Square Garden is well-known for its biometric

insights.claim: In one documented instance, Madison Square Garden security tracked a specific fan's movements at a Knicks game down to the minute — cataloging where they went, who they spoke with, when they ate and where they sat.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Minute-level behavioral tracking of a named individual is the concrete abuse example that carries a bill; it is the kind of detail that survives into legislative findings.
insights.quote: MSG security tracked the movements of a specific fan at a Knicks game down to the minute, cataloging their movements, who they spoke with, when they ate, and where they sat.

insights.claim: Hundreds of lawyers involved in disputes with James Dolan or Dolan-owned properties have been banned from his venues, including a mother blocked from taking her daughter to a Radio City Music Hall show.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Blanket exclusion of opposing counsel converts a security system into a litigation-strategy tool — a novel liability surface for entertainment-venue owners.
insights.locator: Hundreds of lawyers involved in disputes with Dolan

insights.claim: Madison Square Garden maintains a database assigning risk scores to roughly 400 celebrities and VIPs, with some dossiers including attendees' race and sexual orientation.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Storing race and sexual orientation alongside risk scores is exactly the sensitive-category processing that draws regulatory penalties in most biometric and privacy regimes.
insights.quote: MSG also maintains a database that assigns risk scores to around 400 celebrities and VIPs. Some of the dossiers also include the race and sexual orientation of those who attend the arena.

insights.claim: Madison Square Garden filed a defamation lawsuit against WIRED in July 2026, in the same month WIRED published its report on MSG's celebrity risk-scoring database.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Suing the outlet rather than disputing the practice signals MSG intends to fight disclosure legally, raising the odds this becomes a press-freedom flashpoint that amplifies rather than suppresses the story.
insights.quote: MSG filed a defamation lawsuit against WIRED later that month.

insights.claim: Madison Square Garden's public defense of its facial-recognition program is that automated face matching is merely an electronic version of ordinary human recognition, a framing that concedes no distinction between one-off recognition and persistent databased identification.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: This 'it's just recognition' framing is the industry's core legal argument against biometric bans; if it fails in New York, expect it to fail elsewhere.
insights.quote: “People have been recognizing each other’s faces since the beginning of time—we just do it electronically,” an MSG spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
insights.locator: People have been recognizing each other's faces

insights.claim: Bill sponsor Shahana Hanif cites James Dolan's long relationship with President Donald Trump as an aggravating factor in who controls the biometric data collected on New York venue attendees.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: Politicizing the data custodian broadens the coalition beyond privacy advocates, but also makes the bill a partisan target — watch for state-level preemption attempts.

insights.claim: Hanif argues that AI and security tools marketed to cities on a safety rationale are in practice making residents less safe, an explicit rejection of the security-value proposition vendors sell to municipalities and venues.
insights.speaker: Kate Taylor
insights.so_what: If the 'safety' justification loses political credibility, municipal and venue demand for surveillance-AI procurement contracts erodes at the source.
insights.quote: “New Yorkers need to understand, right now, between AI and all these tools that are being sold to us as being for … our city’s safety, are actually making us less safe”
insights.locator: New Yorkers need to understand, right now
